speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Hello everyone. Welcome to a new episode of The Dissenter. I'm your host, as always, Ricardo Lops, and today I'm joined by a return guest, Dr. Omar Bartov, Dean's Professor of Holocaust and Genocide studies at Brown University, and today we're going to talk about his latest book, Israel What Went Wrong. So Dr. Bartov, welcome back to the show. It's always a big pleasure to everyone.

speaker: Omer Bartov
words: Thanks for having me here again.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Uh, OK, so one of the things I would like to focus on today and you also explore in your book is, uh, Zionism. So what is, uh, Zionism or what was it originally? BECAUSE then we can get into how it might have changed over time and some misconceptions that people have about it.

speaker: Omer Bartov
words: So Zionism is a movement that began in the late 19th century and it was influenced by many other national movements of that period. It's a movement that assumed that the, the Jewish people, which had existed in one form or another in Europe and in the Middle East and other parts of the world for A couple of millennia was a nation or that could be made into a nation. Most of the Jews of the world at that time, about 80% of the Jews in the entire world, were living in East Central Europe, and they were coming under increasing pressure because of the growth of ethno-nationalism around them, one of whose attributes was also the growth of anti-Semitism. And so what Zionism proposed was that the Jews, like all other groups, form themselves into a nation, claim self-determination as a nation, and then find a place in which they could then implement that idea and create a state or some kind of political entity for themselves. And the territory that Zionism proposed would be where the Jews would create their own state was the ancestral homeland, mythical, historical, of the Jews in what was then Palestine, which at the time in the late 19th century was part of the Ottoman Empire. And as of the early 1880s, small numbers of Jews who increasingly refer to themselves as Zionists start coming to the Ottoman Empire to settle, not as religious Jews, but as the carriers of a new national movement called Zionism. So that's the beginning of Zionism at the time. It was certainly not the most popular movement among Jews. Most Jews who were coming under increasing pressure and violence in Russia, in Ukraine, in Eastern Europe, uh, and also were deeply impoverished, uh, made other decisions. That is, about 2.5 million Jews left East Central Europe and went to North America between the early 1880s and World War I. But increasingly as it becomes more difficult for Jews to migrate, the United States closes off its borders after World War I, and in Europe there is growing resentment against immigrants, especially with the economic crisis. As a result of that, Zionism becomes more popular, as well as the growth of political anti-Semitism that appears to be increasingly threatening for Jews in Europe. And so Zionism from the end of World War I to the outbreak of World War II becomes a much more popular movement and brings several hundreds of thousands of Jews from Europe, mostly from East Central Europe, to Palestine.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: When was it that Israel's independence or the formation of the state of Israel became intertwined with Palestinian displacement or the displacement of Palestinian people?

speaker: Omer Bartov
words: So one part of this process that I described is that when Jews start coming to Palestine, uh, which becomes, uh, comes to be called Palestine under the British Mandate after World War One and becomes under the British, the so-called mandate, which is uh permission that the uh that Britain gets from. THE international community to rule over Palestine and cause it that once Jews start coming there, even before World War I, this begins to create a conflict between the indigenous population, Arabs living there who are increasingly referred to as Palestinians or speak of themselves as Palestinians, and these new immigrants from the point of view. Of the Palestinians, as the numbers of Jews grow, the way they experience it is that they are experiencing settler colonialism, that people are coming from Europe and settling the land and encroaching on their own lands and claiming that that's their territory. So the friction between Jews coming to Palestine who believe that they're coming home to their ancestral homeland. And Palestinians who live there who say, well, that's where we live, and you're taking over our land begins from the very beginning. And it's interesting because there were Jews living there before, but the Jews living in Palestine before that were living there as, as, as local communities and were not making national claims. They were, they were Ottoman citizens, and they were part of the society there. The conflict grows as the numbers of Jews grow, and Jewish settlement in Palestine in the 1920s and 1930s is supported by the British. The British in 1917 issued the Balfour Declaration. Which promises that Britain, then the largest empire in the world, would facilitate the creation of a Jewish national home in Palestine. They don't exactly explain what a Jewish national home is. It's kind of open to interpretation, but eventually it becomes the idea of creating a Jewish state, and they helped the Jews create the infrastructure for a future state in Palestine in the 1920s and the early 1930s. So that creates more and more friction between Jews and Palestinians. Uh, THAT comes to a head, of course, eventually in 1948, because in 1947, The British after World War II declared that they no longer want to be the mandatory power in Palestine. They don't have the energy. They don't have the manpower, resources. They're exhausted after World War II. They're fed up with all the friction in Palestine. They want to leave and they hand over Palestine to the UN, the newly established UN, and the United Nations offers a partition resolution. Uh, uh, United Nations on, on November 29th, 1947, uh, decides that Palestine will be divided into two states, a Jewish state and an Arab state. The leadership of the Jewish community, which numbers then about 600,000 people, accepts that petition. It it accepts it reluctantly because it thinks that it's being offered too little. It's being offered just over half of the territory of Palestine. And the leadership of the Palestinians and the Arab states surrounding Palestine reject it because they say it's unfair because 2/3 of the population of Palestine are Palestinians and they're being offered less than half of Palestine. And that leads to the creation of a Jewish state, not a Palestinian state, and to a war that breaks out in 1948. In the course of that war, The Israeli military, which is being established and then becomes the so-called Israel Defense Forces, the IDF, ethnically cleanses most of the Palestinians in that territory. And so by the end of that war with the ceasefire agreements of 1949, A state of Israel is created in which the majority of the population are Jews and the majority of the Palestinians who had lived there become refugees.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Do you think it's fair to say that over time Zionism has evolved into what is now an ethno-nationalist and settler colonialist ideology? Do you think that's a fair characterization?

speaker: Omer Bartov
words: So first of all, Zionism was always an ethno-national movement. It's it didn't evolve into an ethno-national movement. It was an ethno-national movement, that is, it was a movement that claimed that a particular ethnos, Jews, are a nation, and according to the logic of that, such nations deserve a place of their own. This was not a Jewish invention. This was all around. That's what the polls said, Ukrainians, Latvia, Estonians, whoever. Germans, this was a European invention and and the Jews latched on to that partly because they were victims of this process as a minority in all the countries in which they lived. When you create an ethno-national state, one instinct is that you identify. The people who do not belong to your ethnos but who live in that state as outsiders to your state as a minority. That's how minorities were invented. They were invented by the creation of ethno-national states. Before that they were not minorities. They were just different groups living in a particular territory. So it's always been that. But until 1948, and as I write in the book, Zionism has two faces. One face is of an ethno-national movement that claims a particular territory and exercises precisely that sort of dynamic of saying this is our land, we want to be a majority here. The other people who live here should be a minority, although in fact they are a majority. And there needs to be some mechanism as to how do we make ourselves into a majority. The The plan the Zionists have is that more and more Jews would come from Europe until Palestine becomes a Jewish majority state. But in the Holocaust, most of the Jews of Europe are murdered, and so those people who were expected to create a Jewish majority state are no longer there to make that possible, and that is the sort of underlying logic of the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians. That's the other mechanism. Again, it, it wasn't invented only by Zionism. Ethnic cleansing has been carried out by many other national ethno-national movements, but in this case, it's the Zionists who carried it out in 1948. After the establishment of the state, this one phase of Zionism, which is to say we are here to provide a safe haven for the Jews of Europe. And in many ways that's true. In the 1920s and 1930s when hundreds of thousands of Jews come to Europe, that's how they're saved. Those Jews who stayed in Europe were largely murdered. That includes my own family, both, both my, my grandparents who came in the 1920s and 1930s to Palestine. The rest of their families, my families whom I never knew, were all murdered because they stayed in Poland. So that argument of Zionism seems logical, but Zionism has another face, and that face is from the point of view of Palestinians of settler colonialism, that is, those people who come, including my grandparents, functionally act as settler colonial encroachers on Palestinian land. In 1948, when the state is established, and that's my argument in the book, the state has a choice to make. It promises. Uh, IN its declaration, in its proclamation of a state, it promises to be a, a, an equal state for all its citizens. That all those Jews and Arabs, men and women, all those who become citizens of the state will have equal rights. Now he does that because the UN demands that in order to recognize it as a state. It also promises to issue a constitution. That would reflect the spirit of that proclamation of the state, and it's supposed to do that within a few months. The proclamation of the state is in May 1948, and it says by October 1st, 1948, we'll issue a constitution, and we are still waiting for that constitution. A constitution was never issued by the state, was never adopted by the state, and so the state never actually enshrines in law a commitment to equal rights to all its citizens and never determines in any document what its final borders are. It only has ceasefire lines. It doesn't have any borders that it recognizes as the final borders. And that decision not to have a constitution means that Zionism becomes at that point a state ideology, because now there's a state, and the only thing that drives it is Zionist ideology. Right,

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: when nowadays people identify themselves as anti-Zionist and they say that they are anti-Zionist because they oppose the settler colonialist actions performed by the state of Israel, and they oppose ethnic cleansing of the Palestinian people. speaker: Omer Bartov
words: Uh, OK, that's, that's a big question. So as you can understand from my previous answer, um, I think that Zionism historically is a movement that you can support or not support, you can like or not like. Um, I personally am, I am not a great supporter of any nationalism of any kind because nationalism has brought about a huge amount of destruction to human lives, to cultures. Around the world, uh, but it is what it is. It's something that happens, so to say I'm opposed to that is, is well and fine, but I don't know exactly what it means. We live today in a world of nations. Try living outside of a nation in this world. Think of migrants. If you don't have a passport, if you don't have citizenship, then you are a ship adrift the ocean. You have nothing, uh, and so it's, it's easy to say, well, I'm against it, but what is your alternative? Uh, SO in that term to say I'm an anti-Zionist, you can say I'm anti-Portugal, I'm anti-Spain, I'm anti-France, it's, it's, it's a meaningless term, uh, and I find that to be a kind of cheap label that people now stick on their sleeve because it's sort of become. Um, POPULAR to say that. On the other hand, Zionism as it has evolved and as it exists today as the state ideology of Israel is completely insupportable for all the reasons that you mention. It has become a violent racist, Jewish supremacist, ethnic cleansing, genocidal movement. It's an ideology and it's an that ideology of Zionism in many ways like other ideologies, you know, uh, Portugal had a dictatorship, uh, Italy had fascism, Nazi Germany had Nazism. With the fall of the dictatorship in Portugal, no one said, let's break up Portugal. It doesn't have a right to exist, but the dictatorship didn't have a right to exist and was thankfully done away with after many decades. In Italy, no one said Italy should just go away to the dung heap of history. They said fascism should. And so in that sense, Zionism today has no viability. Anyone who today proclaims their loyalty to Zionism must admit that they are supporting an ideology that has supported genocide. And if you support an ideology that supports genocide, well, you have to look at yourself in the mirror and say, is this something that I can support? Does that mean that Israel can continue to exist as a state? I think Israel will continue to exist as a state. It's not going anywhere. Just like the Palestinians are not going anywhere despite all the claims by Israeli politicians and ideologues that they have to go, that they don't belong, all that kind of nonsense, but it has to redefine itself, as many countries in the 20th century did when they rid themselves of these ideologies. And in the case of Israel, in order to redefine itself, it has to go back to the beginning. It has to go back to precisely that moment of 1948. It has to give itself a constitution. It has to define its borders. It has to accept the wrongs that it committed in 1948 all the way to Gaza, and in many ways Gaza is an extension of what happened in 1948. It's a second attempt to ethnically cleanse the Palestinians. People in Israel spoke about it as being the second Nakba, the second catastrophe for Palestinians. They spoke about it in positive terms. That's what we want to do to them. It has to go back to that and rethink how that territory, which is now one state. There are no two states there. It's one state between the Jordan and the sea. How does that state redefine itself as a place where the equal numbers of 7 million Jews and 7 million Palestinians can share that space, and dreams of getting rid of one group or the other are genocidal, whether they come from the left or the right, whether they come from Palestinians or Jews. They're not the only humane. ACCEPTABLE resolution of this to my mind is to find a way for those people who live there to share the space rather than to dream about kicking them out.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: What is it like to grow up in Israel, serving the IDF, for example, and be exposed to these state and settler colonialist ideology? speaker: Omer Bartov
words: Look, I'm, I'm, I'm 72, so my experience is very different from the experience of younger cos of Israelis. When I was born and raised, uh, Israel was a very small state, uh, that was before 1967, um, and, um, the discourse of, uh, about the nature of the state. And the reality of living in Israel were very, very different from that of later generations. My, my eldest son is now almost 40 years old. He has no idea. What pre-1967 Israel was like. So for later generations, even the notion of the so-called green line, that is, which was the ceasefire line of 1949, which defined the borders of Israel between 1949 and 1967. They have no clue what that is. The, the idea that Israel was once a country between 1948 and 1967, where the majority of people were actually Jews, only 20% of the population were Palestinians, they don't know about that. They, they, they've never lived in a country that is not an occupying country. So, uh, if you ask about my experience, my own experience was very different, and in some ways, that's why. It is difficult for me and I think for many people of my generation in Israel, especially those who grew up in left-leaning homes, who grew up in secular homes, who grew up in homes where there were ideals of social justice and national justice, to look at Israel today and to recognize it. It feels like a completely foreign country. Uh, NOW that does not mean that I did not imbibe, uh, in my childhood and in school, a particular Zionist ideology. I should say that, you know, thinking about it, uh, when I was growing up, we never thought about ourselves as Zionists. We didn't even think of ourselves as Jews. We were Israelis. Zionism was a kind of term that was used by the old people who made all these big speeches that we found really boring. We were just born there and we thought it was our place, and it took a long time for us, because of our education, for people of my generation to start recognizing. That, you know, I was born in the mid-1950s, less than 10 years after the expulsions of the expulsion of the Palestinians, to realize that we grew up in a country in which there were very few Arabs because they had been kicked out. No one spoke about it at the time. There were empty villages and nobody said how were they emptied? What happened there? So yes, for members of my generation, it took a long time and many never went through that process of recognizing that the state was established on a major act of injustice, that it was born in sin. It's not, again, it's not the only country that was born in sin, but that's a particular sin of that particular country. For younger generations, this is a very different situation that we're seeing today. Israel has become Uh, much more religious than he was when I was growing up there, including the army, is much more religious, and the religion that people have now has almost nothing to do with the kind of religion that my grandparents believed in, the kind of traditional Judaism that they had, and they were both Orthodox Jews, both, both sides of my family. Now it's a messianic Jewish supremacist, anti-democratic, violent type of Jewish religion that no Jew around the world living outside of Israel could ever endorse. Uh, AND so, um, the, the, the way that Israelis think of themselves today is very, very different, and I'll say one last important thing, you know, when I was, I left Israel in 1989, uh, and I had served in the military, both as a regular soldier and then as a reservist, and I did serve in occupied territories, but these were the very early years of the occupation. The formative experience of generations of Israelis has been to act as occupiers, as colonizers, and that has really changed the mentality of society vis a vis Palestinians. It has created the process of dehumanization of Palestinians, of thinking of them as people who should be bossed around, who don't have rights, who shouldn't have rights, who don't even have the right to have rights. Uh, AND so that sort of long-term process, uh, is in many ways the result of the long-term occupation that Israel has exercised for most of its existence.

They were not particularly militant. Well, of course they did become militant. In 1982, Israel invaded southern Lebanon, took over the southern part of Lebanon which is populated by Shiites. And that the resistance to Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon, of the Shiite part of Lebanon, produced Hezbollah, which is a Shiite resistance resistance group supported of course by Iran. It has to provide a different political horizon for them. So the Supreme Court. Of the state of Israel, which was being supported by all these protesters on the eve of October 7th because of the attempt by the state to change the rules of the game, that very Supreme Court, which had established the apartheid regime now forbids even using the term in Israel. words: So look, I mean, I think there are two answers to this. There's a sort of short term and a much deeper response. It cannot be a Jewish and democratic state as long as it is not purely Jewish. That's the core reason for the ongoing violence between Israel and its neighbors.

speaker: Ricardo Lopes
words: Right, but, but I mean, just to reemphasize the second part of my question, do you think that this kind of attitude of Israel toward its neighbors in the Middle Eastern region can ever lead, I, I mean, of course, if it stays on this trajectory of continuous war, can it ever lead to stability in the region?

speaker: Omer Bartov
words: No, look, I mean, but obviously war is instability, so as long as you have war, you have instability. STABILITY comes when you stop war. And that would serve their interests, not for love of Zionism or Jews, but because Israel has shown itself to be a resilient country and is supported by very powerful allies, so it's good for everyone. Israel has refused to do that. And it's refused to do it again because of course it would like to have peace with Saudi Arabia. To our populations around the world, in countries which are mostly authoritarian and which worry about the popular sentiment in the countries that they rule, the Palestinians are appealing to those people to come to their rescue. If you go back there, if you, uh, I would say compel Israel for its own good. To find a way to share that space with Palestinians that will resolve the issue of conflict between Israel, not so much with its neighbors because it's not fighting other Arab countries. The last war Israel fought with Arab armies was in 1973. That's the war that I was in. But the militants who are fighting against the Israeli occupation of their own lands.
